en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Section on the Indivisible,
from the Chapter of Puzzling Questions.
4. The Question on Escape from the Snare of Death “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘Neither in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean...’”
“Not by entering a cleft in the mountains,
nor does that region of the world exist where one might stand and escape the snare of Death.”
Furthermore, the Blessed One taught the protective discourses (*paritta*).
They are as follows:
the Ratana Sutta, the Metta Sutta, the Khandha Paritta, the Mora Paritta, the Dhajagga Paritta, the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, and the Aṅgulimāla Paritta.

"If, venerable Nāgasena, one is not released from the snare of death even when gone into the sky, even when in the midst of the ocean, or even when situated in a palace, a hut, a cave, a grotto, a mountain cleft, a ravine, a mountain fissure, or between mountains, then the efficacy of protective charms (*paritta*) is false. If, however, by the performance of protective charms there is release from the snare of death, then that statement—'Not in the sky...

[not] in the midst of the ocean... not by entering a cave... not by swift flight... not by standing on the peak of Mount Sineru... not even by the power of knowledge can one escape the messengers of Death;
wherever one stands, there the snare of Death ensnares one'—is also false."
“This too is a double-edged question, more knotty than a knot, which has come to you;
it must be resolved by you. “Great King, this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One: ‘Not in the sky... [not in the ocean...

not by the power of asceticism can one escape the snare of Death. And protective charms (*paritta*) were taught by the Blessed One, but those are for one whose life-span is not yet exhausted, who is in the prime of youth, and who is free from the obstruction of kamma. There is no action or remedy, Great King, for the prolongation of the life of one whose life-span is exhausted.”
Just as, O Great King, when a thousand jars of water are poured upon a dead tree, a withered stump, devoid of sap,
whose life-force has ceased and whose lifespan has expired, it would neither become moist nor sprout green leaves— even so, O Great King,
there is no means by which medicine or protective charms can effect the prolongation of the life of one whose lifespan is exhausted.
Or medical treatment: Great King, whatever medicinal herbs and remedies there are on this earth, they too are ineffective for one whose life-span is exhausted.

But, Great King, a protective chant (paritta) protects and guards one whose life-span remains, who is endowed with youth, and who is free from the obstruction of karma; it is for such a person's sake that protective chants were taught by the Blessed One.

"Great King, just as a farmer, when his grain is ripe and the stalks are ready for harvest, would prevent the entry of water; yet that crop which is still young, cloud-like, and in its prime flourishes through the increase of water—even so, Great King, the recitation of protective charms and medicines is set aside and rejected for one whose lifespan is exhausted.
However, those protective charms and medicines are recited for the benefit of those people who still have a remainder of life and are in their prime."
“They grow by means of limited medicines.
“Venerable Nāgasena, if one whose lifespan is exhausted dies, while one whose lifespan remains lives, then in that case, protective charms and medicines are useless.
“But, Great King, have you ever seen before anyone whose illness was turned back by medicines?”
“Yes, venerable sir, hundreds have been seen,” [the king replied].
“In that case, Great King, the statement that ‘the administration of medicinal charms is useless’ is false.
“Venerable Nāgasena, the efforts of physicians—such as the drinking of medicines and the application of ointments—are seen, and by those efforts the disease is turned back.”
“Great King, when even the *paritta* chants are being recited, their sound is heard; the tongue dries up, the heart falters, and the throat becomes distressed.
Yet, by the power of that recitation, all diseases are pacified and all calamities depart.

But have you ever seen before, Great King, anyone bitten by a snake who, while the poison was being counteracted by the words of a mantra, was vomiting the poison and spitting it out from both above and below?”
“Yes, venerable sir, even today that [practice] continues in the world.
“In that case, Great King, the statement that ‘the performance of protective charms and medicinal treatments is useless’ is false.
For, Great King, when a man has performed a protective charm, a snake wishing to bite him does not bite him; it closes its open mouth.”
Even the clubs hurled by thieves do not strike; having released their clubs, they show affection.
Even an enraged elephant, upon approaching, becomes calm. Even a great mass of blazing fire, upon coming near, is extinguished.
Even the *halāhala* poison, when consumed, turns into an antidote, or it functions as nourishment. Even executioners who desire to kill [fail to do so].
“Having approached, they become slaves; even when stepped upon, the snare does not release.

But have you not heard this before, Great King: ‘When a peacock had performed a protective chant (*paritta*), the hunter was unable to set the snare for seven hundred years, but when he had not performed the protective chant, he set the snare on that very same day’?
“Yes, venerable sir, it has been heard; that report has spread throughout the world with its devas.”
“In that case, Great King, the statement that ‘the practice of protective charms and medicine is useless’ is false.
Have you not heard before, Great King, how a *dānava*, while protecting his wife, placed her inside a casket, swallowed it, and carried her within his belly;
and then how a certain *vidyādhara* entered through the mouth of that *dānava*?”
“He enjoys himself with her; when that Dānava realized this, he opened the casket after vomiting it out.
As soon as the casket was opened, the Vidyādhara departed according to his pleasure.
“Yes, Bhante, it is heard; that sound has resounded throughout the world with its devas.”
“Was not that vidyādhara, O Great King, released from capture by the power of a *paritta*?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In that case, O Great King, the power of a *paritta* exists.”

"But have you not heard before, Great King, that another Vidyādhara, having become deeply infatuated with the chief queen in the inner palace of the King of Bārāṇasī, vanished in an instant by the power of his incantations upon being seized?
"Yes, venerable sir, it is so heard.
"Was not that Vidyādhara, Great King, released from capture by the power of a protective charm (paritta)?"
“Yes, venerable sir,” he replied.
“In that case, great king, there is such a thing as the power of a protective charm.
“Venerable Nāgasena, does every protective charm protect everyone?”
“Great King, it protects some, but it does not protect others.
“In that case, venerable Nāgasena, the protective chant (paritta) is not universally effective.
“But, Great King, does food protect the life of everyone?”
“Venerable sir, some guard it, while others do not.
“For what reason?
“Because, venerable sir, some die of cholera after eating that very same food in excess.”
“In that case, Great King, does food not protect the life of everyone?

“For two reasons, venerable Nāgasena, food takes away life: either by being eaten in excess, or by weakness of heat. Food, venerable Nāgasena, which gives life may take away life through improper treatment.
“Even so, Great King, a protective charm protects some and does not protect others.”
"By three causes, Great King, a *paritta* does not protect: by an obstruction of karma, by an obstruction of defilements, and by lack of faith.
A *paritta* that protects beings, Great King, abandons its own protective power through what has been done by oneself;
just as, Great King, a mother nourishes her child while it is still in the womb, gives birth with beneficial care, and having given birth, removes the impurities, filth, and mucus."
“Suppose a woman anoints herself with the finest, most excellent perfumes; yet at a later time, when others’ sons revile or strike her, she strikes them back.
They become angry with her, drag her before the assembly, seize her, and bring her to her husband—provided, however, that her son has committed an offense and transgressed the bounds.

Then the husband’s men, dragging her away, beat and batter her with sticks, clubs, knees, and fists. Now, Great King, would her mother receive such dragging, hounding, seizing, and being brought before her husband?”
“No indeed, Bhante.
“For what reason, Great King?
“Because of my own transgression, Bhante.”
“In the same way, Great King, a protective charm intended for the protection of beings is rendered fruitless by one’s own fault.

“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! This question has been well analyzed; the thicket has been cleared, darkness has been turned into light, and the web of views has been disentangled—you have achieved this by relying on the most excellent assembly of the Saṅgha.
The fourth question: On being released from the snare of Death.
